khajuraho: A ghee-rich platter of dal, kadhi, seasonal sabzi and hot rotis, the everyday food of Bundelkhand.
Wheat balls baked on coals, broken into hot dal and drowned in ghee, with garlic chutney on the side.
Sweet shops near the bus stand
Fluffy poha with sev and onion, followed by a hot crisp jalebi. Central India's favourite morning pairing.
Earthy laddoos made from the flower of the mahua tree, a Bundelkhand and Gond speciality.
Light and sound show at the Western Group
After dark the temples glow and the story of the Chandela kings is told over their carvings.
pachmarhi: The Madhya Pradesh breakfast: soft poha topped with sev, then a syrupy jalebi straight from the pan.
Local eateries on the main road
Grated corn slow-cooked in milk and spices, a Malwa classic that tastes best on a cool evening.
Baked wheat balls dunked in ghee and eaten with spicy dal and chutney.
Dhoopgarh, the highest point of the Satpuras
At 1,350 m this is the top of central India. Arrive early and watch the plains turn gold.
Bee Falls, a short drive from town
A plunge pool under a clear waterfall, best from July to October when the forest is loud and green.
ujjain: Ujjain starts its day with steaming poha and jalebi, often straight after darshan.
Hot, flaky, dal-stuffed kachori with sweet-and-sour chutney, sold from early morning.
Malwa's baked wheat balls with ghee, dal and a garlic chutney that bites back.
The pre-dawn ash aarti is one of the most intense rituals in India. Book your slot online well ahead.
Glide beneath the island temple shaped like the sacred syllable Om as the river wakes up.
kanha: Baiga and Gond homestays near Mukki
Millet porridge and rotis cooked on a wood fire. Nutty, filling and nothing like city food.
Village stalls near the park gates
Sweet, earthy laddoos from the mahua flower that the Baiga and Gond have made for generations.
A hot, no-frills breakfast to eat before the early morning safari.
Dawn jeep safari for the tiger
Kanha's sal forests and open meadows are where The Jungle Book was imagined. Book the zone and jeep early.
Kanha is the only place that saved the hard-ground barasingha. Look for the stags in the morning mist.
orchha: Dal, kadhi, sabzi, hot rotis and a sweet, served the way Bundelkhand eats at home.
Steamed gram-flour dumplings in a tangy dal, a rustic Bundeli snack you rarely find outside the region.
Sweet shops on the main road
Hot kachori with aloo sabzi, a quick breakfast before the palaces open.
Evening aarti at Ram Raja Temple
Ram is worshipped as a king here, with a daily guard of honour by armed police. Nowhere else does this.
Fourteen cenotaphs of Orchha's kings glow gold above the river while vultures circle overhead.
bhopal: Old city restaurants near Jama Masjid
Rich, slow-cooked mutton in a thick gravy, with a Bhopali twist of local spices. Eat it with sheermal.
Smoky kebabs and tikkas grilled over charcoal in the narrow lane beside the mosque, busiest after dark.
Bhopal's morning ritual: soft poha with a crunchy topping and a jalebi on the side.
A clear, lightly spiced black tea, sipped slowly at a street corner.
Bhopal is the City of Lakes. Take a boat out at sunset and watch the old city lights come on.
darjeeling: Steamed or fried dumplings with a fiery tomato chutney, the signature snack of the hills.
A hot noodle soup that keeps the mountain chill away. Ask for it with chicken or vegetables.
Happy Valley Tea Estate and tea lounges
Delicate, floral and light, picked in spring. Taste it at a tea estate where the leaves grow.
A crisp, ring-shaped rice bread eaten at festivals and with morning tea.
A steam engine puffs through the town streets on a heritage narrow-gauge line. Book ahead in season.
kolkata: A paratha rolled around kebab, egg and onion. Kolkata invented the roll, and the original is still the best.
Crisp shells filled with tamarind water and spiced potato, Kolkata's answer to pani puri.
Old mithai shops in north Kolkata
Spongy cheese balls in syrup, followed by sweet set yoghurt in a clay pot. Both are Bengal's pride.
Mutton slow-cooked in its own dark gravy, best with luchi or rice.
Asia's oldest working electric tram still rattles through the old city. Cheap, slow and full of character.
puri: Rice and dal cooked in earthen pots over wood and offered to the deity, then shared. Sit on the floor and eat it from banana leaf.
Lentils cooked with raw banana, pumpkin and papaya, lightly tempered. It is Odisha's comfort food.
Cottage cheese baked slowly until caramelised and smoky. Lord Jagannath's favourite, they say.
Layered, crisp, syrup-soaked pastry, the best-known temple sweet in Puri.
Fishermen drag in their boats at dawn while the sun comes out of the Bay of Bengal.
sundarbans: Crab straight from the creeks, cooked in a hot Bengali mustard-and-chilli gravy.
The Bengali favourite, fried or in a light curry, with plain rice.
Wild honey collected by honey gatherers (mouals) who risk the forest. Dark, fragrant and unlike any jar at home.
Drift along narrow creeks where the Royal Bengal tiger swims, with crocodiles basking on the mud banks.
Walk through paddy fields and fishing villages at dusk, with a cup of tea in a clay cup.
bodhgaya: Wheat balls stuffed with sattu and roasted on coals, served with smoky mashed brinjal and potato.
Paper-thin, crisp layers of pastry soaked in sugar, a Nalanda-district specialty.
Crushed sesame and jaggery pressed into crisp little discs. Gaya's winter treat.
A hot bowl of noodles in a light broth, a fixture of the Tibetan quarter.
Dawn meditation at the Mahabodhi Temple
Sit under the descendant of the Bodhi tree while chanting rises from the monks around you.
gangtok: Steamed pork, chicken or vegetable dumplings with a hot chilli chutney, available on every street.
Strips of pork fat stewed with radish and dried chillies, a Sikkimese Bhutia classic.
A tangy soup from fermented leafy greens, drunk piping hot on cold evenings.
A ring of crisp, slightly sweet rice-flour bread, a festival regular.
A car-free promenade lined with cafés, shops and live music, where the whole town gathers at dusk.
north-sikkim: Chewy, smoky yak cheese eaten as a snack or cooked in soups. Hard as a rock, delicious, and lasts for hours.
A hot bowl of noodles and vegetables, the best thing at 2,700 m.
Fermented millet in a bamboo mug, topped up with hot water and sipped through a bamboo straw.
Steamed dumplings with chilli chutney, the warming snack of the high valleys.
In April and May the Valley of Flowers blazes red and pink under snow peaks, with hot springs nearby.
pelling: Thin, earthy pancakes of buckwheat flour eaten with ghee or a spicy chutney.
A tangy soup made from hard yak or cow cheese, thickened with local vegetables.
Fermented soybeans cooked into a pungent curry. Strong, but an authentic taste of Sikkim.
The world's third-highest peak glows pink from the ridge above town, if the clouds allow.
Milk tea with a chewy chunk of yak cheese to nibble in between sips.
